questions.question: For a string containing exactly three spaces, `String s = "   ";`, what do `s.isEmpty()` and `s.isBlank()` return?
options: `true` and `true`
`true` and `false`
`false` and `true`
`false` and `false`
questions.explanation: `isEmpty()` is true only when `length()` is 0, and this string has length 3, so it is false. `isBlank()` (Java 11) is true when the string is empty or contains only whitespace, so it is true here. Use `isBlank()` when validating user input such as names that might be just spaces.

questions.question: What three values does this program print?
options: `ditya`, `2`, `true`
`Aditya`, `3`, `false`
`ditya`, `3`, `true`
`dity`, `2`, `false`
questions.explanation: `substring(1)` returns everything from index 1 to the end, so "ditya". `indexOf("ity")` is 0-based: A=0, d=1, i=2, so it returns 2. `compareTo` compares character codes, and `'A'` (65) comes before `'a'` (97), so the result is negative and the check prints `true`.

questions.question: A teammate writes `String code = "abc"; code.toUpperCase(); System.out.println(code);` and is surprised that `abc` is printed. What is the fix?
options: Call `code.toUpperCase(true)` so the change is applied in place
Assign the result: `code = code.toUpperCase();`, because String methods return a new String and never change the original
Use `code.equalsIgnoreCase("ABC")` before printing
Declare `code` as `final` so the method can modify it
questions.explanation: Strings are immutable, so transformation methods like `toUpperCase()`, `trim()` or `replace()` build and return a new String; the notes show `s` pointing to a new "HELLO" object while "Hello" stays as it was. If the result is not stored, it is simply lost. `final` has nothing to do with it, and there is no in-place variant.

questions.question: What are the initial capacities of `new StringBuilder()`, `new StringBuilder(50)` and `new StringBuilder("java")`?
questions.explanation: The no-argument constructor reserves 16 slots, and the `int` constructor uses exactly the capacity you pass (50). The `String` constructor reserves 16 extra slots on top of the text's length, so "java" gives 4 + 16 = 20, as the notes show. Capacity is the reserved space; `length()` is how many characters are actually stored.

questions.question: What does this sequence of `StringBuilder` calls print?
options: `Adoitya`
`oitya`
`oXYya`
`AXYitya`
questions.explanation: `insert(2, 'o')` gives "Adoitya". `delete(0, 2)` removes indices 0 and 1 (end is exclusive), leaving "oitya". `replace(1, 3, "XY")` replaces indices 1 and 2 ("it") with "XY", giving "oXYya". The same builder object is modified at each step, unlike String methods.

questions.question: With `StringBuilder sb1 = new StringBuilder("Aditya");` and `StringBuilder sb2 = new StringBuilder("Aditya");`, why does `sb1.equals(sb2)` return `false`?
options: Because `StringBuilder.equals()` also compares capacities, which differ
Because `StringBuilder` does not override `equals()`, so it uses `Object.equals()`, which compares references
Because `equals()` on a mutable object always returns `false` to be safe
Because the two builders were created in different threads
questions.explanation: `StringBuilder` inherits `equals()` from `Object`, which only checks whether both references point to the same object; these are two separate objects. To compare contents, use `sb1.toString().equals(sb2.toString())` or, since Java 11, `sb1.compareTo(sb2) == 0`. The notes mark `sb1.equals(sb2)` as "true X" for exactly this reason.

questions.question: A single-threaded batch job builds a 100,000-line CSV text with `+=` on a `String` and is slow. Which replacement best matches the lecture's guidance?
options: `StringBuilder`, because it is mutable (appends go into one growing buffer) and has no synchronization overhead
`StringBuffer`, because it is always the faster of the two mutable classes
`String.join` inside the loop on every iteration, because it avoids creating new objects
`new String(...)` around each `+=`, so every piece goes to the heap instead of the pool
questions.explanation: `StringBuilder` appends into an internal array that grows as needed, so it avoids creating a new String per step. `StringBuffer` offers the same API but its methods are synchronized, which adds overhead that a single-threaded job does not need; the notes call `StringBuilder` faster and the usual choice. Wrapping in `new String(...)` just creates even more objects.
questions.source: notes p2, p4 (StringBuilder thread safe X, StringBuffer thread safe; StringBuilder faster)

questions.question: What length and capacity does this program print?
questions.explanation: The builder starts with capacity 16 + 4 = 20. Appending 17 characters needs room for 21, which exceeds 20, so it grows to (old capacity * 2) + 2 = 42, the same rule that turns 16 into 34 in `Demo3.java`. The length is the number of characters actually stored: 4 + 17 = 21.

questions.question: Given `String v = "1.5";`, why does `v.replace(".", "-")` return `"1-5"` while `v.replaceAll(".", "-")` returns `"---"`?
options: Because `replaceAll` also replaces digits, while `replace` only replaces punctuation
Because `replace` stops after the first match, while `replaceAll` replaces every match
Because `replaceAll` works on the `byte[]` value while `replace` works on characters
Because `replaceAll` treats its first argument as a regular expression, and `.` in a regex matches any character
questions.explanation: `replace(CharSequence, CharSequence)` replaces every literal occurrence of the text, so only the dot changes. `replaceAll` (and `split`) take a regex, in which `.` means "any character", so every character is replaced. To match a literal dot in a regex you escape it, e.g. `replaceAll("\\.", "-")`. Both methods replace all matches; `replace` does not stop after the first.

questions.question: Two threads append to the same shared `StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("Hello")`: thread 1 runs `sb.append('A')` and thread 2 runs `sb.append('B')`. Occasionally the result is corrupted (a character is lost or overwritten). What is the right explanation and fix?
options: `StringBuilder` is immutable, so concurrent appends create copies that overwrite each other; use `String` instead
The JVM only allows one `append` per object; call `ensureCapacity()` first
`StringBuilder` methods are not synchronized, so the appends can interleave (a race condition); use `StringBuffer`, whose methods are synchronized
The two `char` values are promoted to `int` and added together; use `append(String.valueOf(c))`
questions.explanation: `StringBuilder` is not thread-safe: both appends can read the same `count` and write into the same slot, which is the race condition in the notes. `StringBuffer` synchronizes its methods, so each append completes fully before the other starts, giving "HelloAB" or "HelloBA" but never a corrupted value. Which letter comes first still depends on thread scheduling.
questions.source: notes p4 (StringBuffer: mutable + thread safety, race condition example)
